name: Suma (Pfaffia paniculata, Brazilian ginseng)
short: Case report of occupational asthma from inhaling suma root dust (a different route). A Cochrane review found no adverse effects reported in one sickle cell trial (low- to very low-quality evidence).
text: A 1991 case report describes a worker who developed asthma after inhaling Pfaffia paniculata root powder used to manufacture capsules, with allergy confirmed by skin testing, a bronchial challenge and specific IgE antibodies; this was workplace inhalation, not taking the product by mouth. A 2020 Cochrane review of plant medicines in sickle cell disease included one trial of a powdered extract of Pfaffia paniculata and reported that no adverse effects were reported with it, rating the evidence low to very low quality; the review abstract does not give the trial's size, length or how adverse effects were recorded. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
